system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 7 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2143-11-20 02:44:00 to 2143-11-26 09:58:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of hypercoagulable state, chronic anticoagulation with Lovenox, stable aortic arch thrombus, and chronic chest and abdominal pain was admitted for worsening pain. The chest pain was pleuritic in nature and non-cardiac, with normal cardiac enzymes and EKG. Abdominal pain was diffuse and severe, and on examination, a new incisional hernia was identified. Surgery recommended outpatient management. Pain was controlled with IV morphine initially, then transitioned to oral oxycodone with acetaminophen. The patient's hemoptysis and tracheobronchomalacia remained stable. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up with surgery for hernia repair, continue all chronic medications, use temporary increased oxycodone for pain, and evaluate a persistent dental issue with a dentist.
problems: Incisional hernia without mention of obstruction or gangrene
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism
Unspecified disorder of the teeth and supporting structures
Embolism and thrombosis of thoracic aorta
Other diseases of trachea and bronchus

radiology_notes.text:
INDICATION:  ___ male with hemoptysis in the setting of factor V
Leiden deficiency and IVC filter.  Comes in with right lower quadrant
abdominal pain.

COMPARISON:  Non-contrast CT of the abdomen from outside hospital from ___.

TECHNIQUE:  64-row MDCT obtained of the abdomen and pelvis from the lung bases
through to the proximal femora.  This study was done with IV and oral
contrast.  Coronal and sagittal displays reviewed alongside axial cuts.

FINDINGS:  The lung bases are clear with no evidence of pleural effusion,
focal consolidation, nodule, or mass.  The heart does not appear enlarged and
there is no pericardial effusion.

The liver enhances homogenously without any focal lesion.  The gallbladder is
normal.  The adrenals are normal bilaterally.  The kidneys enhance and excrete
contrast symmetrically and promptly.  There is a small hypodensity that is
difficult to assess in the prior film without contrast that measures 1.8 x 1.6
cm and does not enhance.  This most likely represents a benign renal cyst. The
pancreas is normal.  Intra-abdominal loops of large and small bowel are
unremarkable.  There is no bowel wall thickening or any signs of bowel
obstruction.  The abdominal aorta is unremarkable.  The celiac, SMA and ___
are both widely patent.  The SMV is patent as well.  Noted in the right upper
quadrant is a small incisional hernia containing omentum at known trocar site.
The neck of this hernia is approximately 1 cm.  A small right upper quadrant
incisional hernia is also appreciated on the film from ___ and is
unchanged.  The patient is status post splenectomy.  Prosthetic mesh seen
repairing ventral wall defect.  No evidence of adhesion of bowel to this mesh
repairing this ventral hernia.  There is no evidence of recurrence of hernia.
There are numerous subcutaneous lesions consistent with changes suggestive of
Lovenox injections.

CT PELVIS WITH CONTRAST:  The distal ureters are seen emptying into the
bladder bilaterally.  There is no evidence of ureteral stone.  The bladder is
partially distended with urine without any thickening of the bladder wall or
filling defects.  The prostate is unremarkable.  The seminal vesicles are
normal.  No inguinal or pelvic lymphadenopathy by CT criteria.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Right upper quadrant small incisional hernia containing omentum, unchanged
from CT from ___.
2.  No additional acute abdominal or pelvic process to account for the
patient's abdominal pain.

INDICATION:  Factor V Leiden deficiency, prior history of pulmonary embolism
and aortic thrombus.  Hemoptysis and tracheobronchomalacia demonstrated on a
bronchoscopy.  Please evaluate tracheobronchomalacia.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric multidetector CT acquisition of the trachea and chest
was performed without intravenous contrast at maximal inspiration and dynamic
forced expiration.  Two attempts were made at dynamic forced expiration as the
initial study did not show adequate decrease in airway caliber.  Images are
presented for display in the axial plane at 1.25-, 5- and 2.5-mm collimation
respectively.  A series of multiplanar reformation images were also submitted
for review.

FINDINGS:  There is no pathologic enlargement of the supraclavicular, axillary
or mediastinal lymph nodes.  The cardiac size is normal without evidence of
pericardial effusion.  There is no pleural effusion.  The central airways are
patent, there is no evidence of an intrabronchial lesion.  

There is no appreciable tracheal or bronchial collapse.  For example, at the

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you're here for worsening right lower quadrant pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago after I moved some heavy furniture. It’s sharp and gets worse with any movement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And is it different from your usual left-sided pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, this is new on the right side. My old pain is usually from the hernia and Lovenox shots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any nausea, vomiting, or fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No nausea or vomiting. I had a low-grade fever once, but nothing consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you’ve been coughing and coughing up blood for about four weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it comes with chest pain when I breathe deeply. It’s been going on for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll look into that. Given your history with blood clots and Factor V Leiden, we need to be careful. We’ve ordered a CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the CT show if it’s another clot or something with my hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help rule out appendicitis, diverticulitis, or a clot. For your hernia, we’ll compare with your prior scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. It shows a small fat-containing incisional hernia in the right upper quadrant, unchanged from before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So is that causing this new pain on the right side?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it’s small. The pain might also be from muscle strain when you lifted. There’s no sign of appendicitis or bowel blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But my pain isn’t getting better with Percocet like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re adjusting your pain meds. We’ll start IV Dilaudid for now and add Tylenol and a muscle relaxant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery for the hernia?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Surgery reviewed your case and recommends holding off. If pain persists in a few weeks, you should follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better with the new meds, but still pretty bad when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding tizanidine, a muscle relaxant, to help with strain. We also need to address your cough and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The hemoptysis worries me. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw 30cc of blood when you were admitted. Given your history, we’re concerned about tracheobronchomalacia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a bronchoscopy before. They said my airway is floppy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re scheduling another bronchoscopy to check if that’s the source of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did the bronchoscopy yesterday. Your airway didn’t collapse much, but we did see severe GERD and friable tissue in the right upper lobe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the bleeding could be from acid reflux irritating my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s likely. We’re increasing your PPI to twice daily to reduce acid and protect your airway.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the blood culture was negative, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no infection found. Your chest X-ray is also clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. What about my pain meds? I still need something stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching your oxycodone to 15mg every 4 hours as needed. But take it with stool softener—we don’t want constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I keep using Lovenox twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. With your Factor V Leiden, stopping anticoagulation is too risky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest vitals are stable. Pain seems better with the new regimen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, more manageable. Still tender, but I can move without screaming.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’re also adding a daily laxative to prevent straining, which could worsen the hernia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Should I stop lifting anything heavy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Definitely. Avoid heavy lifting for now. If pain continues, surgery may reconsider repair.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If pain worsens, or you develop fever, vomiting, or more bleeding, come back. Otherwise, follow up with your PCP in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the oxycodone—how long can I take the stronger dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Until you see your doctor. Don’t drive or drink alcohol while on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pantoprazole twice a day for reflux?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, take it consistently. It helps both your cough and bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any other tests I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lung nodule is stable. Your PCP will arrange a follow-up CT in 12 months due to your smoking history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep that appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Continue all meds, avoid heavy lifting, and follow up with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I still be worried about clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: As long as you stay on Lovenox and move around, your risk is managed. Report any chest pain or leg swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to. No more moving furniture!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart move. Let someone else do the heavy work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge papers are ready. Nurse will go over everything with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is here for you. Take care and stay in touch with your doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're doing well. Just keep following the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make my follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s the best thing you can do right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready when you are.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of Factor V Leiden deficiency, chronic anticoagulation with Lovenox, incisional hernia, and tracheobronchomalacia was admitted for new-onset right lower quadrant abdominal pain and persistent hemoptysis. The abdominal pain, worsened by movement and poorly controlled on prior oxycodone, was evaluated with CT imaging which showed a small, stable incisional hernia without acute findings. Surgery recommended medical management and outpatient follow-up. Pain was managed with increased oxycodone, acetaminophen, and tizanidine. Hemoptysis and chronic cough were assessed with bronchoscopy, which confirmed tracheobronchomalacia and severe GERD, prompting an increase in PPI therapy. The patient improved clinically, was discharged home on optimized pain and reflux regimens, and advised to follow up with primary care and surgery if symptoms persist.
